items.q: A 76-year-old retired schoolteacher presents with a two-year history of insidious, progressive memory decline, frequently misplacing personal items, forgetting family appointments, and repeating identical questions. Physical and neurological examinations are entirely normal. MRI brain reveals prominent bilateral hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy without vascular lesions. In accordance with NICE guideline NG97, what is the recommended first-line pharmacological treatment for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease?
items.exp: NICE guideline NG97 recommends offering an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, galantamine, or rivastigmine) as first-line monotherapy for patients diagnosed with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease. These medications modestly enhance cognitive function, global functioning, and activities of daily living.
r: Correct: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease per NICE NG97.
Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist licensed for moderate Alzheimer disease in patients intolerant of cholinesterase inhibitors, or for severe disease.
Haloperidol is an antipsychotic with no cognitive benefit and carries severe stroke and mortality risks.
Vitamin E lacks clinical trial evidence for improving cognition in Alzheimer disease.
items.kp: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) are first-line options for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease.
items.source: NICE guideline NG97: Dementia: assessment, management and support

x.key: Donepezil, galantamine, or rivastigmine are first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease.

others.B: Memantine is for severe disease or AChEI intolerance.

x.pearl: Before starting an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, check an ECG or resting pulse, as they can cause bradycardia and heart block.
x.clues: Insidious memory loss, hippocampal atrophy, mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease first-line drug.
x.mech: Reversible inhibition of synaptic acetylcholinesterase elevates synaptic acetylcholine levels in the nucleus basalis of Meynert projections.
x.lo: Select the first-line pharmacological treatment for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease.
x.rev: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) are first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease.

items.q: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes presents with cognitive difficulties. His family describes a 'stepwise' pattern of deterioration over the past three years, with abrupt drops in executive ability and decision-making followed by periods of relative stability. Neurological examination reveals mild left-sided spastic hemiparesis and an extensor plantar response. MRI brain reveals extensive periventricular white matter hyperintensities and multiple subcortical lacunar infarcts. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Vascular dementia typically presents with a stepwise, fluctuating clinical progression linked to cumulative ischaemic strokes or subcortical microvascular lacunes. Clinical features include early executive dysfunction, psychomotor slowing, and focal neurological signs (hemiparesis, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars), corroborated by ischemic white matter changes and lacunes on MRI.
r: Correct: Stepwise decline, vascular risk factors, focal pyramidal signs, and lacunar infarcts define vascular dementia.
Alzheimer disease presents with insidious, smooth progressive memory loss without stepwise drops or early focal deficits.
Frontotemporal dementia presents with early disinhibition, personality change, or progressive aphasia in younger patients.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with the triad of gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and dementia with ventriculomegaly.
items.kp: Vascular dementia is characterized by stepwise decline, early executive dysfunction, focal neurological deficits, and ischaemic MRI lesions.
items.source: NICE guideline NG97: Dementia: assessment, management and support

x.key: Stepwise decline, focal pyramidal signs, and lacunar infarcts indicate vascular dementia.

others.C: Frontotemporal dementia has early personality change.
others.D: NPH has gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, ventriculomegaly.

x.pearl: Management of vascular dementia centers on secondary prevention: tight control of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, antiplatelet therapy, and smoking cessation.
x.clues: Hypertension, diabetes, stepwise cognitive decline, focal pyramidal signs, MRI lacunes.
x.ddx: Alzheimer disease with coincidental white matter changes, mixed dementia, multi-infarct encephalopathy.
x.mech: Arteriolosclerosis of penetrating cerebral end-arteries produces chronic subcortical ischaemia and interruptions of fronto-subcortical white matter circuits.
x.lo: Differentiate vascular dementia from Alzheimer disease.
x.rev: Vascular dementia features stepwise cognitive decline, early executive impairment, and focal neurological signs.

next.text: Review NICE NG97 diagnostic criteria for dementia subtypes.

items.q: A 74-year-old man presents with progressive cognitive impairment. His daughter reports that his mental clarity fluctuates dramatically from day to day; on some mornings he is coherent and conversational, while on others he is confused and somnolent. He frequently describes seeing vivid, brightly coloured, detailed images of children and animals playing in his living room. Examination reveals resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and a stooped, shuffling gait. What is the diagnosis?
items.exp: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is diagnosed clinically by the core triad of: (1) fluctuating cognitive function with pronounced variations in attention and alertness, (2) recurrent, well-formed, detailed visual hallucinations, and (3) spontaneous motor features of Parkinsonism (rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor).
r: Correct: Fluctuating cognition, vivid visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism define dementia with Lewy bodies.
Alzheimer disease does not feature prominent early visual hallucinations, marked fluctuations in alertness, or spontaneous parkinsonism.
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease causes rapid fatal cognitive decline over weeks/months with myoclonus and periodic sharp waves on EEG.
Progressive supranuclear palsy features early vertical gaze palsy, axial rigidity, and frequent early backward falls.
items.kp: Dementia with Lewy bodies presents with fluctuating cognitive alertness, recurrent vivid visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism.
items.source: NICE guideline NG97 / McKeith consensus criteria for DLB

x.key: Fluctuating alertness, detailed visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism define DLB.

others.B: Alzheimer lacks early hallucinations and parkinsonism.
others.C: CJD is rapidly fatal over weeks with myoclonus.

x.pearl: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out vivid dreams during sleep) frequently precedes the onset of DLB by years or decades.
x.clues: Fluctuating daytime alertness, vivid visual hallucinations of children/animals, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor.
x.ddx: Parkinson disease dementia (motor symptoms precede cognitive decline by >1 year), Alzheimer disease, delirium.
x.mech: Cytoplasmic alpha-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies) deposit in cortical and subcortical neurons, causing loss of dopaminergic and cholinergic terminals.
x.lo: Recognise the core clinical diagnostic triad of dementia with Lewy bodies.
x.rev: Dementia with Lewy bodies features fluctuating cognition, detailed visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism.

next.text: Review McKeith consensus criteria for DLB.

items.q: A 75-year-old man with newly diagnosed dementia with Lewy bodies is admitted to an acute medical ward with a chest infection. He becomes distressed and agitated at night, believing strangers are in his room. The on-call junior doctor considers administering haloperidol. Why are first-generation antipsychotics like haloperidol strictly contraindicated in patients with dementia with Lewy bodies?
o: Severe, potentially fatal neuroleptic sensitivity (extreme rigidity, sudden immobility, and autonomic collapse)
Risk of precipitating acute pulmonary haemorrhage
items.exp: Patients with dementia with Lewy bodies have extreme neuroleptic sensitivity (affecting up to 50% of patients). Exposure to typical (first-generation) antipsychotics like haloperidol can trigger catastrophic worsening of parkinsonism, 'lead-pipe' rigidity, prolonged sedation, autonomic collapse, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and substantially elevated mortality. Haloperidol is strictly contraindicated.
r: Correct: Extreme neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB can cause catastrophic motor worsening, rigidity, and death.
Antipsychotics do not cause acute pulmonary haemorrhage.
Antipsychotics do not cause direct optic nerve atrophy.
Antipsychotics do not cause acute nephrolithiasis.
items.kp: Antipsychotics (especially first-generation agents like haloperidol) are strictly contraindicated in DLB due to severe, fatal neuroleptic sensitivity.
items.source: NICE guideline NG97: Dementia: assessment, management and support

x.key: Haloperidol is contraindicated in DLB due to life-threatening neuroleptic sensitivity.

others.C: No link to optic nerve atrophy.

x.pearl: If an antipsychotic is unavoidable for severe distressing psychosis in DLB after non-pharmacological failure, low-dose quetiapine or pimavanserin under specialist guidance is preferred.
x.clues: Dementia with Lewy bodies, agitated, contraindication to haloperidol.
x.ddx: Parkinson disease psychosis, delirium superimposed on dementia.
x.mech: Profound baseline dopaminergic loss in the substantia nigra renders striatal circuits exquisitely vulnerable to catastrophic blockade by D2 antagonists.
x.lo: Explain the life-threatening danger of neuroleptic sensitivity in dementia with Lewy bodies.
x.rev: Haloperidol is strictly contraindicated in dementia with Lewy bodies due to severe, fatal neuroleptic sensitivity.

next.text: Review safe prescribing in Lewy body dementia.

items.q: An 82-year-old man with newly diagnosed mild Alzheimer disease is prescribed donepezil 5 mg once daily. Which vital sign or cardiac parameter must be checked before initiation and during dose titration due to the cholinergic mechanism of this medication?
o: Resting pulse rate (for bradycardia or heart block)
items.exp: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) enhance vagal cholinergic tone on the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. This can cause symptomatic bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome, sinoatrial block, and syncope. Clinicians must verify resting heart rate and history of cardiac conduction disorders prior to initiation.
r: Correct: Check resting pulse rate because cholinesterase inhibitors cause bradycardia, heart block, and syncope.
Pupillary checks alone are insufficient to monitor cardiac cholinergic toxicity.
Routine serum troponin is unindicated in the absence of acute chest pain.
Continuous core body temperature monitoring is not required for donepezil.
items.kp: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia, AV block, and syncope; verify heart rate prior to initiation.
items.source: British National Formulary / NICE guideline NG97

x.key: Check pulse for bradycardia/heart block before starting acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

others.B: Pupils alone miss cardiac conduction risks.

x.pearl: Patients taking beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers alongside donepezil have an compounded risk of severe symptomatic bradycardia.
x.clues: Donepezil started for Alzheimer, vital sign monitoring rationale.
x.ddx: Vasovagal syncope, orthostatic hypotension, sick sinus syndrome.
x.mech: Elevated acetylcholine stimulates cardiac muscarinic M2 receptors, hyperpolarizing nodal pacemaker cells and prolonging AV conduction.
x.lo: Identify bradycardia and conduction abnormalities as safety risks of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.
x.rev: Monitor heart rate for bradycardia and heart block when initiating acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

next.text: Review BNF warnings on donepezil cardiac safety.

items.q: An 80-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease has an MMSE score of 8/30 and is completely dependent on carers for feeding and dressing. She previously had to stop donepezil due to severe gastrointestinal distress and syncope. Which medication acting as an uncompetitive N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist is recommended for severe Alzheimer disease per NICE guideline NG97?
items.exp: NICE guideline NG97 recommends memantine monotherapy for patients with severe Alzheimer disease, or for patients with moderate Alzheimer disease who are intolerant of or have contraindications to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Memantine is an uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist that modulates excessive glutamatergic excitotoxicity.
r: Correct: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist recommended for severe Alzheimer disease or AChEI intolerance.
Galantamine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, which would also be contraindicated or poorly tolerated in this patient.
Selegiline is an MAO-B inhibitor used in Parkinson disease, not standard for severe Alzheimer disease.
Amantadine is an antiviral/dopaminergic agent, not indicated for Alzheimer disease.
items.kp: Memantine is an uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist indicated for severe Alzheimer disease or patients intolerant of cholinesterase inhibitors.
items.source: NICE guideline NG97: Dementia: assessment, management and support

x.key: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist indicated for severe Alzheimer disease.
x.pearl: Memantine can also be added as combination therapy to an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor in patients with moderate or severe Alzheimer disease.
x.clues: Severe Alzheimer disease (MMSE 8/30), intolerant of AChEIs, NMDA receptor antagonist.
x.mech: Blocks pathological tonic levels of glutamate activation of NMDA receptors without interfering with physiological synaptic transmission.
x.lo: Identify memantine and its mechanism in the treatment of severe Alzheimer disease.
x.rev: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist indicated for severe Alzheimer disease.

items.q: A 56-year-old previously respectable bank manager is brought for medical assessment by his spouse. Over the past 14 months, he has exhibited dramatic personality changes: making vulgar sexual remarks to strangers, shoplifting small items without guilt, bingeing exclusively on sugary doughnuts, and showing complete apathy when his brother passed away. Formal memory testing shows relatively preserved short-term recall. What dementia subtype is suspected?
items.exp: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) typically presents in younger individuals (under 65 years) with prominent early changes in personality, social conduct, and interpersonal behaviour (disinhibition, loss of empathy, apathy, hyperorality/dietary changes, compulsive behaviours), while episodic memory and visuospatial skills remain relatively intact in early stages.
r: Correct: Early disinhibition, hyperorality (sugar bingeing), apathy, and preserved memory define behavioural frontotemporal dementia.
Alzheimer disease presents with prominent early episodic memory impairment with preserved social manners.
Vascular dementia presents with stepwise decline and focal neurological signs on a background of vascular disease.
Dementia with Lewy bodies presents with visual hallucinations, fluctuating alertness, and parkinsonism.
items.kp: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presents in middle age with personality changes, disinhibition, hyperorality, and preserved memory.
items.source: NICE guideline NG97: Dementia: assessment, management and support

x.key: Early disinhibition, dietary sugar bingeing, apathy, and preserved memory define bvFTD.

others.B: Alzheimer has early episodic memory loss.
others.D: DLB has visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.

x.pearl: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are ineffective in frontotemporal dementia and may paradoxically worsen behavioural agitation.
x.clues: Middle-aged man, disinhibition, sugar craving, apathy, preserved short-term memory.
x.ddx: Late-onset bipolar mania, major depressive pseudodementia, antisocial personality disorder.
x.mech: Selective degeneration and atrophy of frontotemporal lobes linked to tau pathology (Pick disease) or TDP-43 inclusions.
x.lo: Recognise the clinical presentation of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.
x.rev: Frontotemporal dementia presents with early disinhibition, loss of social decorum, and hyperorality.

next.text: Review diagnostic criteria for frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

items.q: An 82-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease residing in a care home develops new-onset agitation, shouting, and resistance to personal care in the evenings. What is the mandatory initial clinical approach in accordance with NICE guideline NG97 before considering any psychotropic medication?
o: Explore and treat underlying physical causes (pain, urinary tract infection, constipation, sensory impairment) and employ non-pharmacological de-escalation
Immediately initiate oral haloperidol 5 mg twice daily
Restrain the patient physically to prevent wandering
items.exp: NICE guideline NG97 mandates that for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), clinicians must first conduct a comprehensive assessment to rule out treatable physical triggers: pain, constipation, urinary retention or tract infection, dehydration, medication side effects, or uncomfortable environments. Non-pharmacological interventions and environmental adjustments are the essential first-line management.
r: Correct: Rule out physical causes (pain, UTI, constipation) and try non-pharmacological care first per NICE NG97.
Haloperidol should not be prescribed routinely and carries high mortality and stroke risks.
Benzodiazepines cause sedation, worsening confusion, and increase falls/fracture risk.
Physical restraint is harmful, unethical, and prohibited in routine dementia care.
items.kp: In behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), rule out physical triggers (pain, UTI, constipation) before psychotropic medication.
items.source: NICE guideline NG97: Dementia: assessment, management and support

x.key: Investigate physical causes (pain, infection, constipation) before psychotropic drugs in BPSD.
x.pearl: The mnemonic 'PINCH ME' summarizes reversible triggers for delirium and BPSD: Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment.
x.clues: Dementia care home resident with acute agitation, mandatory first step.
x.ddx: Delirium superimposed on dementia, sensory deprivation, depression.
x.mech: Impaired communicative ability in dementia causes unmet physical needs (such as pain from arthritis or full bladder) to manifest as behavioral distress.
x.lo: Describe the first-line assessment and non-pharmacological management of BPSD.
x.rev: Investigate and treat physical triggers (pain, infection, constipation) before considering medication in BPSD.

next.text: Review NICE NG97 BPSD management algorithm.

items.q: A 69-year-old retired civil engineer is evaluated for progressive cognitive decline over 8 months. His wife reports that his walking became slow and unsteady, with a wide base and 'magnetic' shuffling as if his feet are glued to the floor. Over the past two months, he has developed urinary urgency and frequent incontinence episodes. Brain CT reveals marked symmetrical ventricular enlargement out of proportion to cortical sulcal enlargement. What potentially reversible condition is this?
items.exp: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) classically presents with Adams-Hakim clinical triad: gait disturbance (typically the earliest and most prominent sign, magnetic/shuffling), cognitive impairment, and urinary incontinence ('wet, wacky, and wobbly'). Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy on neuroimaging confirms the diagnosis, and symptoms can improve following cerebrospinal fluid diversion (ventriculoperitoneal shunting).
r: Correct: Magnetic gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and dementia with ventriculomegaly define normal pressure hydrocephalus.
Alzheimer disease features prominent early memory loss without early magnetic gait or urinary incontinence.
Parkinson disease features asymmetrical resting tremor and rigidity without prominent ventriculomegaly.
Multi-infarct dementia features focal deficits and lacunar infarctions.
items.kp: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with the triad of magnetic gait disturbance, dementia, and urinary incontinence ('wet, wacky, wobbly').
items.source: NICE guideline NG97 / British Journal of Neurosurgery

x.key: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, and dementia with ventriculomegaly indicate NPH.

others.B: Alzheimer lacks early gait and urinary triad.

x.pearl: A diagnostic high-volume lumbar puncture (CSF tap test, draining 30-50 mL of CSF) showing objective gait improvement predicts a positive response to ventriculoperitoneal shunting.
x.clues: Magnetic shuffling gait, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline, ventriculomegaly.
x.ddx: Binswanger disease, Parkinson disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, vascular dementia.
x.mech: Impaired CSF resorption at arachnoid granulations expands ventricles, stretching periventricular sacral motor fibers of the corticospinal tract.
x.lo: Recognise the classic clinical triad and neuroimaging findings of normal pressure hydrocephalus.
x.rev: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with gait disturbance, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence.

next.text: Review reversible causes of cognitive decline.

items.q: A care home physician is requested to prescribe risperidone for an 84-year-old resident with vascular dementia who wanders into other residents' rooms at night but is not distressed or aggressive. Why does NICE guideline NG97 emphasize that antipsychotics should not be used for mild behavioural symptoms in dementia unless there is severe distress or immediate risk of harm?
o: Antipsychotics in dementia confer significant excess risks of ischaemic stroke and all-cause mortality
Antipsychotics consistently induce fatal hypoglycaemia in dementia
Antipsychotics lead to irreversible aplastic anaemia
Antipsychotics precipitate immediate blindness in vascular dementia
items.exp: Large-scale randomized trials and regulatory warnings (MHRA / FDA) demonstrate that antipsychotic use in older adults with dementia is associated with a three-fold increased risk of ischaemic stroke and an elevated risk of all-cause mortality, alongside accelerated cognitive decline and extrapyramidal symptoms. NICE NG97 restricts their use strictly to severe aggression, agitation, or psychosis causing severe distress or danger.
r: Correct: Antipsychotics in dementia significantly increase the risk of stroke, accelerated cognitive decline, and all-cause mortality.
Antipsychotics do not cause fatal hypoglycaemia.
Aplastic anaemia is a very rare idiosyncratic reaction (clozapine/carbamazepine), not the routine warning for risperidone in dementia.
Antipsychotics do not cause immediate blindness.
items.kp: Antipsychotics in dementia carry significant risks of ischaemic stroke, accelerated cognitive decline, and increased all-cause mortality.
items.source: MHRA Drug Safety Update / NICE guideline NG97: Dementia

x.key: Antipsychotics in dementia increase risks of ischaemic stroke and all-cause mortality.
x.pearl: If an antipsychotic is deemed essential for severe distress or violence, it should be prescribed at the lowest licensed dose and reviewed every 6 weeks to attempt tapering.
x.clues: Dementia resident wandering without distress, warning against antipsychotics.
x.ddx: Non-pharmacological approaches, environmental modification, pain management.
x.mech: Impaired cerebral autoregulation, orthostatic hypotension, sedation-induced immobility, and prothrombotic vascular effects promote cerebrovascular events.
x.lo: Explain the safety warnings regarding antipsychotic prescribing in patients with dementia.
x.rev: Antipsychotic use in dementia carries a proven increased risk of stroke and mortality.

next.text: Review MHRA safety warnings on antipsychotics in dementia.
